lessons.title: Harshad Mehta and the 1992 Securities Scam

body.text: Harshad Mehta did not simply out-trade the market. He diverted money from the banking system into shares, and prices rose on money that was never his to invest. When the source was exposed, the rally collapsed.

children.text: If you have watched the series Scam 1992, you know the outline of this story. This lesson goes beyond the drama to the mechanics: the loophole in the banking system that made it possible, how borrowed bank money fuelled one of the steepest bull runs in Indian history, how a single newspaper report brought it down, and why almost every safeguard you rely on as a Zerodha-era investor, from your demat account to T+1 settlement, traces back to what happened in 1992.
India in 1991: A Market Waiting for a Spark

In July 1991, facing a balance of payments crisis, India began opening its economy. Licences were scrapped, foreign investment was welcomed, and a sense of possibility swept through Dalal Street. That was a genuine displacement. But the market that greeted it was primitive by today's standards. Shares existed as paper certificates that had to be physically delivered. Brokers traded by shouting on the floor of the Bombay Stock Exchange. And SEBI, set up in 1988, only received statutory powers through an ordinance on 30 January 1992, just months before the scam broke.

points: Trading by open outcry on the BSE floor
Paper share certificates, open to forgery, loss and delays in transfer
Settlement in fortnightly cycles, allowing large positions to be carried without paying
A young regulator that had only just received statutory powers
Brokers acting as middlemen in banks' government securities deals

columns.label: Today
points: Screen-based electronic trading on NSE and BSE
Shares held electronically in demat accounts with NSDL or CDSL
T+1 settlement: shares and money move the next working day
A powerful SEBI with investigation, surveillance and penalty powers
Banks' securities transactions settled through RBI systems, not brokers' accounts

children.text: The Loophole: Ready Forward Deals and Bank Receipts

markDefs.definition: The minimum share of a bank's deposits that it must hold in safe, liquid assets, mainly government securities. Banks that fall short must buy more securities.

Short-term transactions in which one bank sells government securities to another and agrees to buy them back at a fixed price on a set date. Economically, it is a secured short-term loan, similar to a repo.
A document issued by a bank confirming that it had sold securities and was holding them on behalf of the buyer. It was supposed to be backed by real securities.

children.text: Banks in India must invest a portion of their deposits in government securities under the
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
. In the early 1990s, banks that temporarily needed cash or securities to meet this requirement used
ready forward deals
with each other, often arranged through brokers. Instead of physically handing over securities, the selling bank frequently issued a
bank receipt (BR)
, a piece of paper stating that the securities existed and were being held for the buyer.
That piece of paper was the loophole. In simplified form, here is how the money flowed:
Bank A wants to buy government securities for a short period. A trusted broker offers to arrange the deal.
Bank A pays the money into the broker's account, instead of directly to the selling bank, because the broker is seen as a reliable intermediary.
The broker gives Bank A a bank receipt from another bank, confirming the securities exist. Some of these receipts were issued by smaller banks without any real securities behind them.
For days or weeks, the broker has hundreds of crores of bank money in his account, and uses it to buy shares.
When the deal is due to reverse, the broker repays Bank A using fresh money from the next bank deal, or from profits on shares that have risen.
As long as share prices keep rising and new bank money keeps arriving, nobody notices that the securities never existed.

body.text: Strip away the paperwork and this is the leverage and forced seller story from Chapter 1. Very short-term money, borrowed from banks, was used to make bets on shares. The scheme only worked if prices kept rising and the banks never asked to see the securities. The moment one bank demanded its money back, the whole structure was at risk.

body.title: Why Did the Scheme Work for So Long?
body.question: Why were brokers able to use bank money for share purchases for months without being caught?
options: SEBI had approved the practice in 1991
Banks relied on bank receipts instead of checking real securities, paid money into brokers' accounts, and saw rising share prices keep repayments flowing
The Reserve Bank of India had stopped supervising banks
The money came from foreign investors, not Indian banks
body.explanation: The scheme depended on trust in paper. Banks accepted receipts as proof that securities existed, routed money through brokers' accounts, and did not reconcile what they actually held. Rising share prices let brokers repay each deal on time, so nothing looked wrong. Weak internal controls, not a single rule, allowed the fraud to grow.

children.text: The Big Bull Run

With bank money flowing in, Harshad Mehta bought heavily into a handful of stocks, and the rest of the market followed. The media called him the Big Bull. Retail investors, many investing for the first time, rushed in to buy whatever he was said to be buying.

stats.label: Sensex, April 1992
stats.context: The peak of the scam-fuelled rally

stats.label: Rise in About a Year
stats.context: One of the fastest rallies in Sensex history

body.title: Your Turn: The ACC Rally
body.prompt: ACC's share price rose from about ₹200 to about ₹9,000 during the 1991 to 1992 bull run. By what percentage did it rise?
body.explanation: Rise = (9,000 ÷ 200 minus 1) × 100 = 4,400%. The share price multiplied 45 times. ACC was a well-established cement company, and nothing in its business changed by 45 times in a few months. A price move completely disconnected from the business is one of the clearest signs that something other than fundamentals is driving the market.

children.text: The Unravelling

In April 1992, State Bank of India discovered a large shortfall in its government securities holdings linked to transactions routed through Harshad Mehta. On 23 April 1992, Sucheta Dalal, a journalist at The Times of India, reported that about ₹500 crore of SBI's money had been diverted. As investigators dug deeper, the numbers kept growing, and the banks that had funded the rally demanded their money back. Brokers were forced to sell shares to repay them, and the rally reversed.

body.title: The 1992 Securities Scam and Its Aftermath

events.title: Economic Liberalisation
events.description: India launches sweeping economic reforms, setting off optimism and rising share prices.

events.title: SEBI Gets Statutory Powers
events.description: An ordinance gives SEBI legal authority to regulate markets, formalised by the SEBI Act later that year.

events.title: The Peak
events.description: The Sensex reaches about 4,467, having risen roughly 274% in a year.

events.title: The Story Breaks
events.description: Sucheta Dalal reports in The Times of India that about ₹500 crore of State Bank of India funds had been diverted through securities transactions.

events.title: Investigations Begin
events.description: The RBI-appointed Janakiraman Committee and a Joint Parliamentary Committee investigate, and the CBI takes up criminal cases. Harshad Mehta is arrested later that year.

events.title: The Market Crashes
events.description: The Sensex falls to about 2,529, roughly 43% below its April peak.

events.title: A New Kind of Exchange
events.description: NSE, incorporated in 1992, launches fully automated screen-based trading, forcing a transformation in how India trades.

events.title: The End of Paper Shares
events.description: The Depositories Act is passed and NSDL begins dematerialising shares.

events.title: Mehta Dies in Custody
events.description: Harshad Mehta dies of a heart attack aged 47, while in custody at Thane prison, with many cases still pending.

events.title: Justice, 25 Years Later
events.description: Four former bank officials are sentenced to three years in jail in a 1992 scam case, showing how long these trials dragged on.

stats.label: Irregularities Estimated
stats.context: In broker-mediated ready forward deals, per the Janakiraman Committee

stats.label: Criminal Charges Against Mehta
stats.context: Along with more than 600 civil suits

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The journalist whose Times of India report on 23 April 1992 exposed the diversion of State Bank of India funds was Sucheta ___.
body.explanation: Sucheta Dalal's reporting, later expanded with Debashis Basu in the book The Scam, is a reminder that investigative journalism is part of a market's defences. The initial ₹500 crore figure turned out to be a small part of a much larger fraud.

children.text: Who Lost Money, and How

The losses fell on those least able to see them coming. Retail investors who joined the rally late bought near the top: an investor who put ₹1 lakh into a portfolio tracking the Sensex at its April 1992 peak would have seen it fall to about ₹56,615 by August. Banks that had paid money against worthless receipts faced huge losses, and some of the smaller banks that had issued receipts were ruined. Genuine companies saw their share prices crash along with the manipulated ones, and trust in the stock market was badly damaged for years.
The Reforms That Built Today's Market

The scam exposed almost every weakness in India's market plumbing at once. The response over the next decade rebuilt that plumbing. Each safeguard below is something you use, often without noticing, every time you place an order.

cells: SEBI given statutory powers in 1992, and strengthened repeatedly since
SEBI investigations, surveillance, penalties and orders against manipulators
NSE launched screen-based trading in 1994, and BSE followed with its own electronic system
A live, transparent order book on apps like Zerodha Kite
Paper shares open to forgery and bad delivery
Depositories Act 1996, with NSDL and later CDSL
Shares held electronically in your demat account
Long settlement cycles that let positions build up unpaid
Move to rolling settlement, shortened step by step
Brokers holding and moving other people's money
Stricter rules on client funds, securities and margins
Exchanges send you direct statements of your funds and holdings, so you can check what your broker reports

body.title: Watching Scam 1992? What to Keep in Mind

children.text: The 2020 series Scam 1992 is based on the book The Scam by Sucheta Dalal and Debashis Basu, and it brought this history to millions of new investors. It is worth watching, with a few cautions:
It is a dramatisation.
Dialogue, characters and some events are compressed or invented for storytelling. Use the book and contemporary reporting for facts.
Allegations are not findings.
The scam involved many people and institutions, and not every allegation made at the time was proven in court. Mehta himself was convicted in only some of the cases against him before his death.
The hero framing is misleading.
Charismatic market figures make compelling television, but the real lesson is how people who trusted a charismatic figure lost money.

body.title: The Stock That Only Goes Up
body.scenario: A Telegram channel with 2 lakh members has been recommending a little-known smallcap stock. It has hit the upper circuit on 14 of the last 20 trading days and is up 380% in two months. There has been no major company announcement. The channel admin says "big operators are accumulating, target 5x" and posts screenshots of members' profits. Your friend wants to invest ₹1.5 lakh.
body.prompt: Using lessons from 1992, what warning signs do you see, and what would you check before your friend invests?
body.modelAnswer: Almost every warning sign from 1992 is present. The price has multiplied with no change in the business or any disclosure, just as ACC rose 45 times without a matching change in fundamentals. The rally is tied to an "operator" rather than to earnings, and the only evidence offered is screenshots of other people's profits, which proves nothing. Repeated upper circuits in a small stock can mean there are few sellers and thin liquidity, so it may be very hard to sell when the mood turns. Before investing, check: whether the stock is under NSE and BSE surveillance measures such as ASM or GSM, which exchanges use to flag unusual price moves; its free float, trading volumes and recent bulk and block deals on the exchange websites; its shareholding pattern for changes in promoter holding or pledges; its results on Screener.in to see whether sales and profits justify any of the rise; and SEBI's website for any orders involving the company or related Telegram channels, since SEBI has acted against pump-and-dump schemes run through such channels. In a pump-and-dump, the promoters of the rally sell to latecomers, and the latecomers are left holding shares that fall sharply. Your friend should treat the tip as a red flag, not a recommendation, and never invest money they cannot afford to lose on a stock like this.

body.title: Manipulation Warning Signs: Check Before You Buy
steps: Compare the stock's price rise over the last three months with any change in sales, profits or company announcements
Check on the NSE or BSE website whether the stock is under an ASM or GSM surveillance framework
Look at the shareholding pattern for low public shareholding, since stocks with a small free float are easier to push around
Check how many days in a row the stock has hit its upper circuit, and whether volumes are unusually thin
Search SEBI's orders for the company's name and for the names of anyone promoting it
Be sceptical of any tip that relies on "operators", guaranteed targets or screenshots of profits
If you believe you have seen a market manipulation scheme, you can report it to SEBI

body.label: SEBI: Enforcement Orders
body.description: Search SEBI's website for enforcement orders against market manipulation and unregistered advisers. Reading a few orders shows how modern pump-and-dump schemes work and how SEBI traces them.

cards.definition: A short-term deal where one bank sells government securities to another and agrees to buy them back later, similar to a repo.
A document confirming a bank had sold securities and was holding them for the buyer. Some BRs in 1992 had no securities behind them.
The minimum share of deposits a bank must hold in safe, liquid assets such as government securities.
The nickname given to Harshad Mehta during the 1991 to 1992 rally he was seen as driving.
The RBI-appointed committee that investigated the 1992 scam and estimated irregularities in ready forward deals at about ₹4,024 crore.
Converting paper share certificates into electronic holdings, made possible in India by the Depositories Act 1996.
A scheme in which manipulators push up a stock's price with hype or coordinated buying, then sell to latecomers.

points: The 1992 scam exploited ready forward deals and bank receipts to divert short-term bank money into shares
Fuelled by that money, the Sensex rose about 274% in a year to about 4,467, and ACC rose from about ₹200 to ₹9,000
Sucheta Dalal's report on 23 April 1992 exposed the fraud, and the Sensex fell about 43% by August 1992
The Janakiraman Committee estimated irregularities of about ₹4,024 crore, and Harshad Mehta faced 72 criminal charges before dying in custody in 2001
The scam drove the reforms behind today's market: a powerful SEBI, screen-based trading on NSE, demat accounts and short settlement cycles
The core lesson still applies: price rises disconnected from the business, driven by a single personality or "operator", are a warning sign, not an opportunity

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute investment or legal advice. It describes a historical case based on public reports, committee findings and court outcomes; figures are approximate. Not every allegation made at the time was proven, and references to individuals are limited to publicly reported facts.
